title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

reading.body:
Instinct is an AI assistant in private testing that connects to users' emails, messaging apps, calendars, and device data to perform tasks like booking appointments and finding flights. The system was deployed with access to sensitive information and the ability to take actions like sending emails without explicit permission for each action. Early testers found the assistant could be phished, could access sensitive codes, and continued summarizing emails after users disconnected its access, showing that access revocation did not work as expected.

The deployment relied on broad terms of service that granted the company perpetual rights to user data for training purposes and made it difficult for users to delete stored information. These failures in permission scope, access control, and data deletion would have required stricter limits on what data the system could access and what actions it could take without explicit per-action authorization, plus verification that access revocation actually stopped all data collection.

It is not established whether the privacy and security issues were known to the company before deployment, whether they resulted from negligence or design choice, or what specific technical fixes are needed beyond tighter access controls.

reports.title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

summary:
# Summary

Instinct, an AI personal assistant still in private testing, is gaining attention for its powerful capabilities but raising significant privacy and security concerns. Created by a team led by former Sierra scientist Noah Shinn, the assistant connects to users' emails, messaging apps, calendars, and device data to perform tasks like booking appointments and finding flights. However, early testers have discovered troubling issues, including overly broad terms of service granting the company perpetual rights to user data for training purposes, difficulty deleting stored information, and the ability to access sensitive codes and send emails without explicit permission.

Several prominent tech figures have publicly criticized the platform's security model and data handling practices. One developer discovered the service could be easily phished, while another found emails continued being summarized after disconnecting access. Users worry about granting AI agents such extensive read and write access to personal accounts. Following these concerns, Instinct announced it is raising a $250 million Series B at a $2.5 billion valuation led by Index Ventures and Benchmark, though the company has not yet publicly addressed the specific privacy criticisms.
